correctness.rationale: The squarefree criterion is p−(D/p) | n−(D/n) at each prime, as in Helmreich–Webster Theorem 2. At n=3qr, reducing the q and r tests gives the two positive quotient integers j and k. Since r−c≥q+1 and 3q−ab≤3q+1, k is 1 or 2; r≤3q+2. Eliminating r gives (jk−9)(q−b)=(3−a)(3b+kc). The right side is nonzero for k=1,2, so q≤1+4(3+k)≤21 and r≤65. A separately written bounded check used trial division through √65 and tested all eight sign triples against all three original divisibilities for each prime pair, 600 cases. It returned (105,−+−), (195,++−), (255,−++), (399,−−−), (561,+++), and (2703,−++), with the listed quotient pairs and prime witnesses 41,109,89,41,157,89 (direct residue-square checks). The frozen VERIFIER.py and logged output were inspected, not executed; /workspace/replays/4.js provides the independent bounded reproduction. CRT gives the desired signs on exactly one eighth of the reduced classes that are 1 mod 4, and PNT in arithmetic progressions gives prime densities 1/8 conditional and 1/16 unconditional for each row. This is not a classification for other prime supports or discriminant families.

originality.rationale: The exact six rows were not found printed together, but the strongest published comparison is not merely Williams' criterion or a table for a fixed discriminant. Helmreich–Webster Theorem 4 gives the same signed two-quotient parametrization for arbitrary preproduct, and §5.2–5.3 gives its exhaustive enumeration including all four sign pairs at the last two primes. Setting the preproduct to 3 and taking both signs at 3 already gives the exact cutoff and enumeration by direct substitution. The additional prime-discriminant density is the standard independent residue-class count for any fixed sign vector, not a new implication particular to these rows.
residual_risks: No independent historical priority assertion is made about who first wrote the six rows together. The strong mathematical implication does not depend on finding the exact values printed as a table.
